Multi-stage sampling

Source: R/design-multistage.R
design_multistage.Rd

Selects clusters at the first stage, then draws rows within them at the second. n is the total across the selected clusters under both allocations, matching design_stratified().

Usage

design_multistage(
  clusters,
  n_clusters,
  n,
  allocation = c("equal", "proportional"),
  min_per_cluster = 0L,
  replace = FALSE,
  na_rm = FALSE,
  size = NULL
)

Arguments

clusters

Column naming each row's cluster.

n_clusters

Number of clusters to select at stage one.

n

Total rows to draw across the selected clusters, at least n_clusters, or a plan from plan_size(). A multiple of n_clusters, no larger than n_clusters times the smallest cluster, gives every selected cluster the same take and every row a closed-form inclusion probability. Otherwise the take depends on which clusters were selected, and draw(weights = TRUE) weights the sample conditional on them. See "When the take depends on the clusters selected".

allocation

"equal" splits n evenly across the selected clusters; "proportional" splits it in proportion to their size, and its weights are conditional on the clusters selected. Proportional allocation can give a small selected cluster no rows; draw() then warns with class drawn_empty_cluster and names it.

min_per_cluster

Minimum rows from each selected cluster. Defaults to 0, and n_clusters * min_per_cluster must not exceed n. A cluster smaller than the minimum is taken whole. draw(weights = TRUE) needs at least 1 under proportional allocation. Take at least two rows per cluster if you intend to estimate a variance: with one, the variation within clusters cannot be measured and ht_total() falls back to the ultimate-cluster jackknife.

replace

Sample with replacement within each cluster? A selected cluster then gives its full share of n however small it is, and a row's inclusion probability is the chance of being drawn at least once, (n_clusters / N_clusters) * (1 - (1 - 1 / N_h)^m) for a take of m from a cluster of N_h rows.

na_rm

Drop rows whose cluster label, or size, is NA instead of raising an error.

size

Optional column holding each cluster's size measure, the same on every row of a cluster: positive, finite and numeric. Clusters are then selected with probability proportional to it. See "Clusters in proportion to size".

Value

A design object, for use with draw().

When the take depends on the clusters selected

Without size, the n rows are split over the clusters selected, so a cluster's take is the same in every sample only under "equal" allocation of an n that divides by n_clusters, with no cluster smaller than n / n_clusters. Otherwise, under "proportional" allocation, with a remainder that goes to the largest clusters selected, or with a small cluster capped at its size and its shortfall dealt to the others, a row's inclusion probability depends on which other clusters were selected. It is the chance of drawing the row given the clusters selected, averaged over every possible selection, which has no closed form, so inclusion_prob() refuses it.

draw(weights = TRUE) weights such a sample conditional on the clusters it selected. With a of A clusters selected and m_i of the N_i rows of cluster i taken, .prob is (a / A) * m_i / N_i, and the estimate of a total is A / a times the sum of the selected clusters' estimated totals. That is unbiased whichever clusters were selected, and so over all of them. ht_total() and ht_mean() estimate its variance with the two-stage formula, the variance between the estimated cluster totals plus that within each cluster at its own take, on a - 1 degrees of freedom, and as_svydesign() hands it to survey in two stages, where the standard errors agree. The variance falls back to the delete-a-cluster jackknife when a selected cluster gives one row of several. Proportional allocation needs min_per_cluster of at least 1 for weights, since a selected cluster with no rows would count as a cluster total of 0.

Clusters in proportion to size

With size, the clusters are selected with probability proportional to a size measure, such as a count of households from a census, by systematic PPS as in design_weighted(): cluster i gets pi_i = n_clusters * M_i / sum(M), and a cluster large enough that this passes 1 is taken with certainty, the rest of n_clusters being spread over the others. Each selected cluster then gives the same m = n / n_clusters rows by simple random sampling, so a row of cluster i, of N_i rows, has inclusion probability pi_i * m / N_i. When the measure is the cluster's row count and no cluster is certain, every row gets n / N: the design is self-weighting, with a fixed number of interviews per cluster.

The measure is a property of the cluster, so every row of a cluster must carry the same value; a cluster with two values is refused. n must be a multiple of n_clusters, and allocation must be "equal".

ht_total() and ht_mean() estimate the variance as Deville's approximation over the estimated totals of the selected clusters below certainty, each scaled by its own 1 - pi_i, plus the variance within the selected clusters, each divided by its pi_i. That is the two-stage estimator of design_multistage() without size when every pi_i is equal. A cluster taken with certainty is a stratum, and adds only the variance of the simple random sample within it. The degrees of freedom count the clusters below certainty less one, and in each certain cluster the sampled rows less one. The variance is declined when one cluster below certainty is selected. With one row taken per cluster, whose variation within clusters cannot be measured, ht_total() falls back to the delete-a-cluster jackknife over the clusters below certainty, with no finite population correction, and declines if a cluster taken with certainty gives one row of several. In simulations of 2,000 draws each from frames of 78 or 80 clusters of 10 to 600 rows, taking 2 or 5 rows from each of 12 or 20 clusters, with and without clusters taken with certainty, the variance averaged 0.94 to 1.02 times the true variance of the total, and 95% intervals covered 93% to 95% of the time.

as_svydesign() hands the design to survey in two stages with Brewer's approximation at the first. A sample with one row from a selected cluster of several goes over in one stage instead, as the clusters of that jackknife, and the standard errors agree. Joint probabilities have no closed form; joint_prob() estimates them with simulate = TRUE.

See also

draw()

Other designs: design_bootstrap(), design_certainty(), design_cluster(), design_reservoir(), design_simple(), design_spatial(), design_spread(), design_stratified(), design_systematic(), design_temporal(), design_weighted()

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:100, site = rep(paste0("s", 1:10), each = 10))
nrow(draw(df, design_multistage("site", n_clusters = 4, n = 12), seed = 1))
#> [1] 12

# Villages selected in proportion to their households, then 5 households
# from each: every household has the same chance, 20 / 260
hh <- data.frame(village = rep(paste0("v", 1:8),
                               times = c(10, 20, 30, 40, 20, 50, 60, 30)))
hh$households <- ave(seq_len(nrow(hh)), hh$village, FUN = length)
pps <- design_multistage("village", n_clusters = 4, n = 20,
                         size = "households")
unique(round(inclusion_prob(hh, pps), 4))
#> [1] 0.0769
